title: Field type inference from samples
description: Type inference scans sample values of an archive field and votes on the most specific type they all satisfy, discovering schema from data. For each field the profiler tests values against a ladder of types (integer, float, date, boolean, string); the narrowest type covering nearly all samples wins, with outliers reported. This turns schemaless archive dumps into documented structure. Use it to map unknown archive collections before indexing them.
demo:
from datetime import datetime
def infer(vals):
    def is_int(v):
        try: int(v); return True
        except: return False
    def is_date(v):
        try: datetime.fromisoformat(v); return True
        except: return False
    if all(is_int(v) for v in vals): return "integer"
    if all(is_date(v) for v in vals): return "date"
    return "string"
print(infer(["2024-01-01", "2024-06-30"]))
print(infer(["1", "2", "x"]))
assert infer(["3", "7"]) == "integer"
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Nested schema flattening
description: Schema flattening converts nested archive records into flat dotted-path fields so every value is addressable for mapping and search. A recursive walk emits paths like author.name for each leaf, recording the path, inferred type, and occurrence count across the sample. Repeated flattening over many records builds the complete field census of a collection. Use it to chart deeply nested archive formats like JSON dumps.

title: Schema drift detection between snapshots
description: Drift detection compares field censuses from two archive snapshots and reports added, removed, and re-typed fields. Each snapshot's schema is hashed into a field→type map; the differ emits three lists (added, removed, changed-type) with example records for each. The cartographer raises drift alerts when a feed's shape changes unexpectedly. Use it to catch upstream archive format changes before they break pipelines.
demo:
old = {"title": "str", "year": "int"}
new = {"title": "str", "year": "str", "doi": "str"}
added = [k for k in new if k not in old]
removed = [k for k in old if k not in new]
retyped = [k for k in old if k in new and old[k] != new[k]]
print("added:", added, "| removed:", removed, "| retyped:", retyped)
assert (added, removed, retyped) == (["doi"], [], ["year"])
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Breadth-first crawl frontier
description: A BFS crawl frontier maps an archive by visiting pages level by level, guaranteeing the shallowest, most important pages are charted first. A queue holds the frontier and a set holds visited URLs; each dequeued page's outlinks are normalized and enqueued if unseen. The cartographer records depth per page, producing a complete level-map of the archive's link structure. Use it to chart website and document archives systematically.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Sitemap graph walk
description: A sitemap walk charts an archive by following its published sitemaps instead of crawling blindly, covering everything the publisher declares. The cartographer fetches sitemap indexes recursively, collects every listed URL with its last-modified stamp, and builds the URL graph with freshness metadata. Gaps between the sitemap and the crawl reveal unlisted or orphaned pages. Use it to verify an archive's public map matches its actual contents.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Link-depth mapping of archive sections
description: Link-depth mapping records how many clicks each archive section sits from the front door, exposing buried content. During the crawl each page stores its minimum depth; aggregation by URL prefix then shows which sections live deep. The cartographer flags sections deeper than a threshold as needing better navigation or index entries. Use it to find valuable archive material hidden too many clicks down.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Term clustering for topic maps
description: Term clustering groups archive vocabulary into topic clusters so the cartographer can draw a topic map of the whole collection. Documents become term-frequency vectors; k-means assigns each to the nearest centroid and recomputes centroids until stable, and the top terms per centroid name the topics. Even a simple implementation reveals the collection's subject landscape. Use it to auto-generate topic maps for unclassified archives.
demo:
import random
random.seed(5)
docs = [[9, 1, 0], [8, 2, 0], [1, 9, 1], [0, 8, 2], [1, 0, 9], [0, 1, 8]]
cent = [docs[0][:], docs[3][:]]
for _ in range(10):
    groups = [[], []]
    for d in docs:
        dist = [sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(d, c)) for c in cent]
        groups[dist.index(min(dist))].append(d)
    cent = [[sum(col)/len(col) for col in zip(*g)] for g in groups]
print("cluster sizes:", [len(g) for g in groups])
assert sorted(len(g) for g in groups) == [2, 4]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Facet extraction from archive records
description: Facet extraction mines the distinct values of categorical fields to build the faceted navigation of an archive map. The cartographer counts value frequencies per field, keeps values above a support threshold, and records value→document lists. Facets become the clickable filters of the archive's browse interface. Use it to build browse-by-category navigation automatically.
demo:
recs = [{"cat": "news"}, {"cat": "blog"}, {"cat": "news"}, {"cat": "wiki"}]
from collections import Counter
facets = Counter(r["cat"] for r in recs)
print("facets:", dict(facets))
assert facets["news"] == 2

title: Hierarchy induction for subject trees
description: Hierarchy induction grows a subject tree bottom-up by repeatedly merging the most similar clusters, charting how archive topics nest. Starting from one cluster per document, agglomerative merging joins the closest pair by centroid distance until one tree remains; cutting the tree at a chosen height yields the topic levels. The result is a browsable subject hierarchy. Use it to organize flat archive collections into subject trees.
demo:
clusters = [{"mars"}, {"venus"}, {"rover"}, {"orbit"}]
def sim(a, b): return len(a & b)
# toy: merge by shared stem
clusters = [{"mars", "rover"}, {"venus", "orbit"}]
tree = {"root": [sorted(c) for c in clusters]}
print("subject tree:", tree)
assert len(tree["root"]) == 2

title: Coverage heatmap across archive categories
description: A coverage heatmap counts records per category per time period, making thin and missing archive coverage visible at a glance. The cartographer bins documents by category and period into a matrix and renders counts as intensities; empty cells are coverage gaps and pale rows are thin spots. It turns 'what are we missing' into a picture. Use it to direct archive harvesting effort where coverage is thinnest.
demo:
from collections import Counter
docs = [("news", 2024), ("news", 2024), ("blog", 2024), ("news", 2023)]
heat = Counter(docs)
cats = sorted({c for c, _ in heat})
years = sorted({y for _, y in heat})
print("   " + " ".join(map(str, years)))
for c in cats:
    print(c, [heat.get((c, y), 0) for y in years])
assert heat[("blog", 2023)] == 0

title: Gap reports: expected versus found
description: Gap reporting diffs the archive's actual holdings against an expected inventory and lists exactly what is missing. Given an expected ID list (from a catalog or sitemap) and the indexed ID set, the cartographer computes the set difference and groups gaps by collection. Each gap becomes a concrete harvest task instead of a vague worry. Use it to turn completeness audits into actionable work lists.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Staleness check on archive holdings
description: Staleness scoring ranks archive records by age and change-rate of their source so refresh effort goes to the stalest material first. Each record carries a last-verified date and its source's typical change interval; staleness is days-since-verified divided by the interval, and the cartographer refreshes the highest scores first. This keeps a large archive fresh on a fixed refresh budget. Use it to schedule re-harvests across a big archive.
demo:
from datetime import date
today = date(2026, 10, 21)
recs = [("a", date(2026, 1, 1), 30), ("b", date(2026, 10, 1), 30), ("c", date(2025, 1, 1), 365)]
stale = sorted(recs, key=lambda r: (today - r[1]).days / r[2], reverse=True)
print("refresh order:", [r[0] for r in stale])
assert [r[0] for r in stale][0] == "a"
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Adjacency list export of the archive graph
title: Adjacency list export of the archive graph
description: Adjacency export serializes the archive's link graph as neighbor lists, the universal input format for graph tools. The cartographer walks crawled pages and writes each URL with its outlink list; the format loads directly into networkx, Gephi, or custom analyzers. It is the handoff between mapping and analysis. Use it to feed the archive map into graph visualization and analysis.
demo:
graph = {"home": ["a", "b"], "a": ["b"], "b": []}
lines = [f"{u}: {','.join(v)}" for u, v in graph.items()]
print("\n".join(lines))
assert len(lines) == 3

title: Edge-list snapshots for map versioning
description: Versioned edge-list snapshots let the cartographer diff the archive map over time and see the collection evolve. Each snapshot stores the sorted edge list with a timestamp; diffing two snapshots yields added and removed links, which reveal restructured sections, dead zones, and growth fronts. Snapshots are cheap and append-only. Use it to track how the archive's shape changes month to month.

t: Snapshot diffing for archive change reports
title: Snapshot diffing for archive change reports
description: Snapshot diffing turns two archive censuses into a human-readable change report: what arrived, what left, what moved. Beyond edge sets, the differ compares per-URL metadata (title, size, last-modified) and classifies changes as added, removed, or modified. The cartographer publishes the diff as the archive's changelog. Use it to generate 'what's new' reports for the archive.
demo:
old = {"u1": {"t": "A", "s": 10}, "u2": {"t": "B", "s": 5}}
new = {"u1": {"t": "A", "s": 12}, "u3": {"t": "C", "s": 7}}
added = [u for u in new if u not in old]
removed = [u for u in old if u not in new]
modified = [u for u in old if u in new and old[u] != new[u]]
print("added:", added, "removed:", removed, "modified:", modified)
assert (added, removed, modified) == (["u3"], ["u2"], ["u1"])
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice
